::: {.key-points}
**Key points**

- GEMMA has added instruments at two sites in the UK DECC atmospheric monitoring
  network: a **carbon dioxide and methane analyser at Jodrell Bank** and a
  **halocarbon instrument at Invergowrie**.
- The additions strengthen atmosphere-based emissions estimates for the **devolved
  administrations**. With four halocarbon instruments now operating, the UK and
  Ireland are the **most intensively monitored countries in the world for halocarbons**.
- Data from the new instruments will be integrated into GEMMA's inverse modelling to
  tighten uncertainty on national and devolved-administration emissions.
:::

## Why this matters

The UK DECC (Deriving Emissions linked to Climate Change) network provides
independent, atmosphere-based checks on greenhouse gas emissions across the UK and
Ireland.

GEMMA has now equipped two additional sites with new instruments:

- **Jodrell Bank (Cheshire):** a Picarro analyser measuring carbon dioxide (CO₂)
  and methane (CH₄)
- **Invergowrie (Scotland):** a Medusa gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer
  measuring more than 40 halogenated ozone-depleting substances and greenhouse gases

These upgrades improve UK emissions estimates, especially outside southern England
and for gases that are hard to quantify from inventory statistics alone. They also
give each devolved administration better evidence for policy.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![Map of the UK and Ireland DECC network showing monitoring sites and the new GEMMA instrumentation at Jodrell Bank and Invergowrie.](/research-highlights/figures/decc-network-expansion-fig1.png){fig-alt="Map of DECC network expansion highlighting Jodrell Bank and Invergowrie."}
:::

## What was installed

### Jodrell Bank: continuous CO₂ and CH₄ measurements

At Jodrell Bank, GEMMA installed a Picarro cavity ring-down spectroscopy analyser
for high-frequency CO₂ and CH₄ observations. Combined with other UK and Irish
stations, the site helps show where emissions come from across England, Wales and
Northern Ireland.

### Invergowrie: expanded halocarbon capability with Medusa GCMS

At Invergowrie, GEMMA installed a Medusa gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer that
measures more than 40 halogenated gases, including hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs),
chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), SF₆, NF₃ and SO₂F₂.
Many are potent greenhouse gases, released from scattered or specialised sources
where inventory estimates can be very uncertain.

### Weybourne: better integration through unified data evaluation

GEMMA is also bringing the **Weybourne** station (run by the National Centre for
Atmospheric Science, NCAS/UEA) into line with the DECC network by using the same
data evaluation processes at every site. This makes measurements from different
stations easier to compare and to quality-control consistently.

## What this means for policy

The network expansion is designed to deliver two outcomes.

1. **More accurate emissions estimates for devolved administrations**

Improved spatial coverage strengthens top-down constraints for emissions from
England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland individually, not only for the UK
total.

2. **Much better estimates of UK halocarbon emissions**

The UK and Ireland now operate **four Medusa systems** (the others are at Mace
Head, Tacolneston and Ridge Hill), more than any other country for these gases.
This coverage means changes in emissions can be detected sooner and checked
against the inventory, giving firmer evidence for climate and air-quality policy.

## What comes next

As data from the new instruments accumulate, GEMMA will use them in its inverse
models to:

- tighten uncertainty ranges on national and devolved-administration emissions
- improve sectoral interpretation of halocarbon trends
- provide independent evidence for UK reporting and mitigation policy
- reduce the latency between emission changes and their detection in the atmosphere
